claims.claim: The 50% Capital Gains Tax discount has been completely abolished for all Australians.
claims.short_explanation: Abolished for assets acquired after 1 July 2027 only. Pre-existing assets use a hybrid system. SMSFs are fully exempt.
claims.detailed_explanation: The 50% CGT discount is not abolished for everyone. It applies only to assets acquired after 1 July 2027. Assets already held will use a hybrid calculation — the old 50% discount applies to gains accrued up to 30 June 2027, and CPI indexation applies after that date. Self-Managed Superannuation Funds (SMSFs) are entirely excluded and retain their one-third discount.

claims.claim: Negative gearing has been fully abolished in Australia.
claims.short_explanation: Negative gearing is NOT abolished. It is restricted for new buyers of established homes only. Three distinct pathways still allow deductions.
claims.detailed_explanation: Negative gearing has not been abolished. Existing property investors keep full deductions. New investors buying established homes post-budget lose the ability to offset rental losses against salary income (losses are quarantined). Investors in new builds retain full negative gearing. Three distinct rules apply depending on when and what you bought.

claims.claim: Self-Managed Super Funds (SMSFs) are completely exempt from the new CGT changes.
claims.short_explanation: Confirmed. SMSFs retain the existing one-third CGT discount and are not subject to the 30% minimum floor or indexation rules.
claims.detailed_explanation: The Treasury and ATO have confirmed SMSFs are carved out entirely from the new CGT framework. SMSFs continue to use the existing one-third discount on long-held assets. The 30% minimum tax floor does not apply to SMSF asset disposals. This is a deliberate policy exclusion to protect retirement savings structures.

claims.claim: Assets purchased before 1985 will lose their full CGT exemption.
claims.short_explanation: Confirmed. Pre-CGT assets (bought before 20 Sept 1985) will have their cost base reset via ATO market valuation on 1 July 2027, ending 42 years of CGT exemption.
claims.detailed_explanation: Assets acquired before 20 September 1985 — including share portfolios — have historically been exempt from Capital Gains Tax entirely. Under the 2026 budget, this legacy exemption ends. The ATO will establish a market valuation of these assets on 1 July 2027 to set a new cost base. Any gains after that date will be subject to the new CPI indexation and 30% floor rules.

claims.claim: These budget changes are already law and will definitely take effect on 1 July 2027.
claims.short_explanation: NOT yet law. Budget measures must pass both houses of parliament. Opposition has flagged a Senate challenge. Consult an accountant before making decisions.
claims.detailed_explanation: Budget announcements are not law. They require legislation to be passed by both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Coalition opposition has indicated it will challenge key provisions in the Senate. Until legislation passes, these remain proposed changes only. Always verify the legal status of any tax change with a registered accountant before adjusting your financial strategy.

claims.claim: Inflation indexation always produces a better CGT outcome than the 50% discount for long-held assets.
claims.short_explanation: Inflation indexation does not guarantee a lower CGT liability. The 50% discount may be more favourable when inflation is high over the holding period, as indexation only adjusts the cost base upward, while the discount directly halves the total gain.
claims.detailed_explanation: While CPI indexation raises the cost base to reflect inflation, it doesn't reduce the taxable gain itself—only the discount method cuts the gain in half. With high inflation over extended periods, the indexed cost base may still leave a substantial taxable gain, making the 50% discount more advantageous in many scenarios.

claims.claim: From 1 July 2027, capital gains will be subject to a new minimum 30% tax rate on all gains.
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum rate applies to real capital gains after inflation indexation, not nominal gains. This means the effective tax rate on nominal gains may be substantially lower depending on inflation and the holding period.
claims.detailed_explanation: The headline '30% minimum tax on capital gains' can be misleading. The 30% floor rate applies to actual economic gains after accounting for inflation through indexation, not the nominal gain amount. For example, a $100,000 nominal gain might only be a $40,000 real gain after inflation adjustment, meaning tax would be 30% of $40,000 rather than $100,000. The effective tax rate on nominal gains can be significantly lower than 30% depending on inflation and how long the asset was held.

claims.claim: A specific budget measure costs $6.4 billion over four years.
claims.short_explanation: ABC News reported a $6.4 billion figure but did not identify which specific budget measure this refers to, making verification impossible without official budget documentation.
claims.detailed_explanation: An ABC News article (13 May 2026) references a budget measure costing $6.4 billion over four years but fails to specify which policy. This could potentially refer to combined CGT and negative gearing reform costs, or another specific measure. Without clarification from official budget.gov.au documentation, the attribution cannot be verified.

claims.claim: Negative gearing removed for all established property investors from 1 July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The claim overstates the scope. Negative gearing is removed only for established properties purchased AFTER 7:30pm on 12 May 2026. Investors who purchased before that deadline likely retain existing negative gearing rights through grandfathering.
claims.detailed_explanation: Multiple credible sources confirm that the government's negative gearing changes apply prospectively to new purchases, not retrospectively to existing investor positions. The policy specifically targets established properties purchased after the 7:30pm budget night announcement on 12 May 2026. Properties purchased prior to this deadline would likely be grandfathered, meaning existing investors retain their negative gearing entitlements. The phrase 'all established property investors' is therefore misleading — it should specify 'all NEW established property investors purchasing after the policy commencement date'.

claims.claim: Division 296 imposes a 15% tax on all superannuation balances exceeding $3 million
claims.verdict_label: Disputed — tax applies to earnings above threshold only
claims.short_explanation: The 15% Division 296 tax does not apply to the entire balance above $3m. It only applies to the earnings (or proportion of income) that relate to the amount by which your Total Superannuation Balance exceeds the indexed Lump Sum Threshold.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997, known as the 'Better Targeted Super Concessions' measure, introduces an additional 15% tax on 'income from superannuation' that relates to superannuation balances above the Lump Sum Threshold (LSBT). The $3 million threshold was set for the 2025-26 income year and is indexed annually in $100,000 increments. Critically, the tax is calculated on the 'proportion of income from superannuation that relates to the amount by which your Total Superannuation Balance exceeds the LSBT' — not on the balance itself or the excess amount in its entirety. This means a member with a $3.5 million balance does not pay 15% on the full $500,000 excess; rather, they pay 15% on the portion of their earnings attributable to that excess, with the calculation based on the income stream's proportion of the total balance that exceeds the threshold. This is a meaningful distinction that significantly affects the actual tax liability for affected members.

claims.claim: 15% tax on all super balances over $3m
claims.short_explanation: Division 296 applies 15% tax only on investment earnings attributable to the portion of total superannuation balance exceeding $3m, not on the excess amount itself nor the entire balance.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim mischaracterises how Division 296 works. Rather than taxing the entire balance above $3m, or even the excess amount itself, Division 296 imposes 15% tax specifically on the earnings and returns (interest, dividends, capital gains) that relate to the portion of an individual's Total Superannuation Balance (TSB) that exceeds $3 million. For example, an individual with $4m in superannuation would only face the 15% tax on the investment returns generated by the $1m above the threshold, not on the $1m principal, the $4m total, or the earnings themselves.

claims.claim: 30% minimum tax on ALL capital gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The claim oversimplifies the policy—the 50% discount is being replaced by inflation indexation, and a 30% minimum tax is introduced, but whether it applies uniformly to all gains remains legally unclear.
claims.detailed_explanation: Budget.gov.au indicates the 50% capital gains discount is being replaced by an inflation-linked indexation method. While a minimum 30% tax rate is introduced, whether this applies uniformly to ALL gains or only to gains above certain thresholds after indexation adjustments remains legally unclear. The phrasing 'on ALL gains' may be an oversimplification that doesn't account for potential exemptions, conditions, or thresholds embedded in the policy. Investors should seek professional legal advice as the precise application remains disputed.

claims.claim: Capital gains will face a new minimum 30% tax rate on ALL gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The minimum 30% rate applies to the inflation-adjusted gain amount, not the total capital gain.
claims.detailed_explanation: The budget reform introduces a minimum 30% tax on gains (not total gains). Under the inflation indexation model, investors calculate the taxable amount as the gain minus an inflation-adjusted cost base. This means the 30% floor only applies to the real/inflation-adjusted gain portion, not the entire capital gain. An investor could effectively pay well above 30% on their actual gain while the 'minimum 30%' only binds to the inflation-adjusted portion.

claims.claim: Inflation indexation always produces a better CGT outcome than the 50% discount for long-held assets
claims.short_explanation: The 50% discount may produce equal or better outcomes depending on inflation rates and individual circumstances.
claims.detailed_explanation: Treasury analysis cited by ABC shows inflation accounted for 56% of ASX 200 share price growth over 10 years to March 2026. This means 44% of gains remain taxable under inflation indexation, while under the 50% discount, 50% of total gains are taxable. For a $100,000 gain at a 47% marginal rate: indexation results in $20,680 tax (44% × 47%), while the 50% discount results in $23,500 tax (50% × 47%). Indexation appears marginally better in this example, but outcomes depend entirely on inflation rates. For very high inflation scenarios (10%+ annually), indexation clearly wins. For lower historical inflation rates, the comparison is less clear-cut and individual circumstances determine which method produces a better outcome.

claims.claim: Capital gains will face a minimum 30% tax rate on ALL gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum tax floor applies only to inflation-adjusted (real) capital gains after cost base indexation, not to nominal gains. Taxpayers whose gains are at or below inflation would owe no CGT.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim oversimplifies the 2026 Budget changes to capital gains tax. Under the new rules taking effect July 2027, the 30% minimum tax rate applies to real capital gains—defined as gains above inflation after indexation adjusts the cost base. The indexation method adjusts the original purchase price for inflation, so if a property purchased for $500,000 is now worth $600,000 but inflation doubled prices, the indexed cost base may be $1,000,000, meaning there is no real gain and no CGT owed. The minimum floor only kicks in where the inflation-adjusted gain exceeds zero. This means the 30% rate does not apply to all nominal capital gains, and gains at or below inflation are not subject to this minimum.

claims.claim: A minimum 30% tax rate will apply to ALL capital gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum floor likely applies only to real (inflation-adjusted) gains, not nominal gains. Gains are first indexed for inflation before the minimum rate applies.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim that a 'minimum 30% tax rate' applies to 'ALL capital gains' may be misleading. Official budget documents indicate the 50% CGT discount is being 'replaced with a discount based on inflation'. This means gains are first adjusted for inflation before the 30% minimum applies. The minimum floor applies to real capital gains (gains above inflation), not nominal (total) gains. This distinction significantly affects tax outcomes: a taxpayer with only inflation-matching gains may not face the minimum floor, while the claim could be interpreted to suggest all gains are subject to the 30% minimum regardless of inflation adjustments.

claims.claim: Division 296 imposes a 15% tax on all superannuation balances exceeding $3 million
claims.short_explanation: The 15% tax applies to earnings on amounts above the $3m threshold, not the entire balance.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 does not impose a 15% tax on the entire superannuation balance for accounts exceeding $3 million. Instead, it applies a 15% tax on the proportion of earnings that relate to the Total Superannuation Balance (TSB) exceeding the $3 million Low Balance Superannuation Threshold (LSBT). For example, a person with a $4 million balance would not pay 15% tax on $4 million — only on the earnings attributable to the $1 million portion that exceeds the $3 million threshold. This is a significant distinction: the tax targets the earnings on excess balances, not the principal amount itself.

claims.claim: 30% tax on ALL capital gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum rate applies to real gains after inflation indexation, not nominal gains. The 'ALL gains' phrasing overstates the impact.
claims.detailed_explanation: Under the announced changes, capital gains will use an indexed cost base method. A retired investor in the 16% marginal tax rate bracket selling a long-held equity portfolio currently faces approximately 8% tax on nominal gains. Under the new rules, the 30% minimum rate applies to real gains (gains above inflation), not the full nominal gain. The phrase 'minimum 30% on ALL gains' is misleading because indexation means only real gains are taxed at the minimum rate, while nominal gains may still benefit from the indexed cost base method.

claims.claim: 30% minimum tax on all capital gains
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum tax rate applies to real capital gains (after inflation indexation), not nominal gains. This is a floor on the effective tax rate on real gains, not a flat tax on nominal gains.
claims.detailed_explanation: The claim oversimplifies the 2026-27 budget tax reform. While the reform does introduce a minimum 30% tax rate on capital gains, this applies after the cost base is adjusted for inflation (inflation indexation). The 50% CGT discount is being replaced with an inflation-based discount. The minimum 30% rate acts as a floor on the effective tax rate on real gains (gains above inflation), not a flat 30% tax on nominal gains. This means if inflation is 3% and your nominal gain is 5%, your real gain is only 2%, and the 30% minimum applies to that 2%, not the full 5%. The mechanism and implications differ significantly from a simple '30% on everything' headline.

claims.claim: 15% tax on all super balances over $3m
claims.short_explanation: Division 296's 15% rate applies only to the earnings portion attributable to the balance exceeding the Low Balance Super Threshold (~$1.9m), not on the entire amount above $3m.
claims.detailed_explanation: Division 296 of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Better Targeted Super Concessions) Act 2023 imposes a 15% tax on the earnings attributable to the portion of an individual's Total Superannuation Balance (TSB) that exceeds the Low Balance Super Threshold (LSBT). For the 2026-27 financial year, the LSBT is $1.9 million. Therefore, a person with a $3 million balance would only face the 15% tax on the earnings attributable to the $1.1 million excess above the LSBT, not on their entire $3 million balance or the $1.1 million excess itself. The tax is calculated on the notional earnings of the excess amount, not a lump-sum tax on the balance.

claims.claim: The minimum 30% tax rate applies to ALL capital gains from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: The 30% minimum tax applies to indexed (inflation-adjusted) capital gains, not necessarily gross nominal gains.
claims.detailed_explanation: Analysis from ASX indicates the 30% minimum floor applies to indexed gains rather than nominal gains. For example, a $100,000 nominal capital gain with $40,000 inflation adjustment would result in the 30% minimum tax applying only to the $60,000 indexed gain, not the full $100,000. This creates a significant distinction between the headline rate and the effective tax on real (inflation-adjusted) gains. Taxpayers may be misled if they expect 30% tax on their full nominal gain when the actual liability may be lower on real gains.

claims.claim: The 50% CGT discount is being replaced by inflation indexation with no choice for taxpayers
claims.short_explanation: The CGT discount is being replaced, but implementation details remain unclear regarding taxpayer choice.
claims.detailed_explanation: Budget.gov.au states the 50% CGT discount will be replaced by 'a discount based on inflation' from 1 July 2026. However, some sources including stockspot.com.au use qualifiers like 'largely' replaced, suggesting nuances may exist. The official budget documentation does not clearly specify whether this replacement is mandatory for all asset types or if some choice remains for taxpayers. Verification is needed to confirm whether all taxpayers must use indexation or can opt for other treatment in certain scenarios.

claims.claim: Capital gains tax changes from the budget take effect from July 2027
claims.short_explanation: While CGT discount changes begin 1 July 2027, negative gearing restrictions commence from 12 May 2026. These are distinct policies with different effective dates.
claims.detailed_explanation: Media reporting has conflated two separate policy changes. Negative gearing restrictions, as reported by ABC News, begin from 'this evening' (12 May 2026), immediately impacting property investors. However, the capital gains tax discount changes take effect from 1 July 2027, giving investors nearly 14 months notice before those changes apply. The budget.gov.au confirms the July 2027 date for CGT changes specifically, while the negative gearing restrictions are a separate, earlier-starting policy.
